claims.text: The initial equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy is a disordered BCC alloy.
The initial equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa.
The initial equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy has limited room-temperature plasticity.
Replacing half of the Mo content with V produces NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5.
Partial replacement of Mo by V reduces the alloy's overall electronegativity contrast.
The Mo-to-V substitution preserves the lattice distortion needed for high yield strength.
NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 can retain a single-phase disordered BCC structure under suitably controlled processing conditions.
CALPHAD can be used to optimize the Mo/V ratio and ensure retention of the single-phase disordered BCC structure.
Controlled cooling rates will produce a homogeneous disordered BCC phase in the V-modified alloy.
A lower electronegativity contrast creates a more uniform electronic environment.
The more uniform electronic environment mitigates localized strong bonding that restricts dislocation motion.
Reducing localized strong bonds improves dislocation mobility and therefore room-temperature plasticity.
The remaining Mo preserves high yield strength through lattice-distortion-induced solid-solution strengthening.
NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 will retain a room-temperature compressive yield strength near 1719 MPa.
NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 will improve room-temperature plasticity by approximately 50% or more relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The beneficial strength-plasticity effect requires retention of a single-phase disordered BCC structure and an optimized Mo/V ratio.
Phase separation or secondary-phase formation may negate the predicted strength-plasticity improvement.

contradictions.description: The boundary limits the hypothesis to specimens that retain a single-phase disordered BCC structure, but the falsification rule treats observation of secondary phases as falsifying the hypothesis rather than as failure to satisfy its stated applicability condition.
